hits.name: Akshay 🚀
hits.text:
RAG is so back!

A new paper shows that straightforward retrieval from chat history can outperform much more complex agent memory systems.

The approach, RAW-RAG, retrieves relevant passages from the original conversation, reranks them, and passes the evidence to an LLM.

Across four benchmarks, it ranked first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark–model settings.

The interesting part is why.

An answer can depend on several connected statements, including what changed, when it changed, and which earlier facts it affects. Turning conversations into isolated memories can break those connections.

RAW-RAG supplied enough evidence to answer more often. Even improved access to the transformed memory stores left an accuracy gap compared with raw evidence.

Preserving the original conversation keeps more of those relationships available for retrieval.

For these memory tasks, that makes simple RAG a baseline that more elaborate systems should have to beat.

paper: https://t.co/HDpy6bkICv

On a related note, I wrote about how observations in agent memory connect facts across conversations to surface patterns an agent can act on. If you’re building agents, you might find that article useful. It’s quoted below.

Split this "one-way door" PR into two:

1. A PR that implements everything, except it can be easily reverted (a two-way door)
2. A followup PR (stacked on top) that actually goes through the one-way door

AKA expand/contract. Use feature flags as needed.

---

Lets you de-risk a huge PR by testing large chunks of it in production first.

Every so often folks ask me "do you still get nervous doing talks"

I have done hundreds of them, and used to be a voice coach and public speaking coach. So you think I'd be used to them by now.

Absolutely not - here is my heart rate data during a 20-minute talk that started at 9:15AM, audience ~600 people.

I brick it beforehand, then peak right as I step onto the stage. I have a Q&A which chills me out (the blue). Then I'm off-stage to chat to folks and answer followup questions.

I doubt this adrenaline response will ever go away. Just got to keep breathing through it.

hits.name: Arpit Bhayani
hits.text:
Tweet ID is a 64-bit integer, but the Twitter API sends it as a string. Here's why...

Twitter generates IDs using Snowflake, which packs a timestamp, a worker ID, and a local sequence counter into 64 bits. Internally, it is a plain integer, which is great for sorting by time and generating IDs across distributed nodes without coordination.

But the problem shows up at the edge - client devices.

When your JS engine parses JSON, it parses numeric value as type Number which is a double-precision floating-point, and hence it can only represent integers exactly only up to 53 bits (because of mantissa width).

Hence, when a browser runs `JSON.parse` on a 64-bit ID, the value is rounded and the ID gets corrupted.

So to with this, Twitter uses a string as the wire format for these IDs. Because a string remains a string across runtimes.

JavaScript does have workarounds, it needs extra work and parsing logic. The problem is that if even one client gets this wrong, the ID gets corrupted again.

Hope you found this interesting :)

hits.name: elvis
hits.text:
Highly recommended read if you work with coding agents. 

My general rule of thumb is to get out of the agents' way as much as I can. 

My top tips from the list:

- Run as many evals as you can; always be constantly measuring, especially on agents' use of knowledge.

- Run as many automations as you can and allow agents to do more proactive work; it's a good way to constantly test and push your agents further. This can even unlock new use cases along the way. I use complex automation to see what breaks, and it helps me find interesting new applications. My automations constantly evolve. 

- Scale agents to do more tasks (either in parallel, batch, etc.) and regularly find out what tools/knowledge they're missing. This is how you really optimize workflows with agents and stay ahead. Yes, a few things will break, but that's for the best, as you can always improve it. The benefit is that you constantly find weak areas to improve and unlock new productivity tricks along the way. But don't blindly do it. Always measure and stay skeptical, but trust that the agent can figure out a lot with the right tools and permissions. Your job is to give it the right tools, context, and knowledge to scale. But how can you know what to give it if you don't actually try to scale anything?

Overall, just be more ambitious in every task you give your agents and get out of the way as much as you can.

hits.name: elvis
hits.text:
Learn to build a custom harness, folks!

There is so much alpha in understanding how to optimize the harness.

This work shows the benefits of a smart harness configuration and caching the decisions your agent harness has already made.

(bookmark it)

They propose HarnessMM, which cuts tokens per task on a DeepSeek harness from 96.28k to 11.62k while success rises from 71.43% to 85.71%.

Harnesses often call the model again after tool feedback even when an earlier call already settled the next action. HarnessMM stores those settled decisions in an Executable Decision Graph with exact actions, arguments, dependencies, and guards. When the guard holds, the controller reuses the decision. Anything new goes back to the model.

A recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop tunes the harness configuration from training feedback, and the model weights never change.

With Codex on HumanEval, success stays at 90.82%, and tokens per task drop 29.54%.

Before you pay for a bigger model, check how many of your harness calls repeat a decision the agent already made.

Paper: https://t.co/HwRNalCUlm

Chat with Paper: https://t.co/DRJZBwHh9J
